title: WTT's money, part one: China's money, and where it actually goes
seo_title: WTT's money part one: who pays for table tennis
description: China pays for the crowds, sponsors and TV audiences behind WTT. But its tournament money does not automatically reach WTT. Part one of two.
standfirst: China supplies the crowds, sponsors and television audiences that make the professional circuit look like a major sport. Tournament takings there do not automatically reach WTT, and the published accounts cannot yet show how much of its revenue depends on China.
body: This is part one of two. Part two, [WTT's money, part two: where it comes from, and what the 2025 accounts show](/news/wtt-finances-ittf-accounts-part-two), covers the 2025 accounts, the 15% shareholding and whether the model can last.

On the first day of the 2024 WTT China Smash at Shougang Park in Beijing, more than 60,000 people came through the gates. On each of the next three days the figure passed 70,000. Those are park visitors rather than ticket holders, and the counts should be read with that in mind, but the scale is the point. In China, table tennis does not need explaining to sponsors or to crowds.

That is the first thing to understand about the sport's money. The second is that the money China produces does not all arrive at WTT's door. The distinction between where a sport's commercial value is made and where its governing company books its revenue explains most of what follows, and the public record leaves the space between the two largely unmeasured.
## A sport organised before it was commercial

Table tennis was run as a federation before it was run as a business. The International Table Tennis Federation was founded in 1926, with its first international tournament held in Berlin in January that year and the first World Table Tennis Championships in London in December. Nine national associations were among its founders. For most of the twentieth century the ITTF was a body of rules and championships, and the sport sat outside the commercial mainstream.

Change came in stages. Table tennis entered the Olympic programme at Seoul in 1988, which gave it a global audience for a few weeks every four years without turning it into a television product. The ITTF introduced a professional circuit, the World Tour, in 1996. In 2017 the federation bought back its commercial rights from the agency that had been managing them on its behalf.

On 30 May 2019 the ITTF announced a new commercial vehicle, World Table Tennis. The first event was held in Macao in November 2020, and in July 2020 WTT signed a long-term partnership with the sports marketing group IMG covering media rights, production, sponsorship sales and betting data. The federation's own account, in a 2025 statement on its accounts, is that WTT was created as a "strategic vehicle to capture the value of our sport and reinvest it for the benefit of all". The Singapore Smash, first held in 2022 as a Grand Smash, became the flagship event outside China.
## China is the market

China's place in the sport's finances is not in dispute. At the 2024 ITTF Annual General Meeting, the minutes record WTT's chief operating officer presenting figures for China: US$34m of income, almost 200,000 spectators at WTT events in China in 2023, 546 hours of television coverage that year and a cumulative television reach of two billion. The minutes do not say over what period the US$34m was earned. They also identify the presenter as chief operating officer of World Sports, a company that press reports later named as WTT's 15% shareholder, which is discussed in part two.

In December 2025 WTT's chief executive, Steve Dainton, told China Daily: "Without China as a huge market, it would be not easy for us to even develop the other parts of the world." He described China as the most significant and biggest market for table tennis.

The commercial value is easiest to see at tournament level. The 2024 China Smash in Beijing was run at Shougang Park. The city government put total box office at close to RMB60m, excluding admission to the park itself. HK01 cites ticket revenue of RMB57m for the same event. Sponsorship was reported at about RMB25m for 2024, and a 2025 report put the sponsorship target for the following year at more than RMB100m. Those are substantial sums for a tournament, and they are reported figures from organisers and the press, not from audited accounts.
## Box office is not WTT's revenue

A Chinese tournament's takings do not automatically belong to WTT. Local organising committees can keep ticket revenue, local sponsorship and other income, depending on the terms agreed with WTT. WTT's own income can come instead as a hosting fee paid by the city or organiser, a share of certain commercial rights, broadcast revenue and tour-level sponsorship. Which of these applies in a given case is set out in agreements that are not published.

Public money is part of the picture. An investigation by the Mail & Guardian into the 2023 WTT Contender in Taiyuan reports, citing a disclosure by the city's sports bureau, that about RMB8.15m of public funds went into the event. About RMB5m of that was a hosting application fee, which is WTT revenue. The prize money was RMB550,000, and the event recorded a loss. The same report says Taiyuan's authorities noted weaknesses in the procurement explanations and contract management. The article does not establish wrongdoing, and the figures are the reported ones.

That example shows how the model can work for a host and still leave the event in deficit. A city can accept a loss for the publicity, the tourism and the prestige, and WTT can still take a fee. Whether that adds up for WTT depends on how much of each event's income the company keeps, and that is the figure the published accounts do not give.

The ITTF's 2025 consolidated statements show total revenue but do not split it by country. The only geographic data is cash held in each currency, which is not revenue. So the question of how much of WTT's revenue depends on China cannot be answered from the published numbers. Eleven checked the statements for any breakdown by market and found none.
## Building the circuit outside China

WTT has been trying to widen its base. The Singapore Smash is the established flagship event outside China. A European Grand Smash was staged in Malmö, Sweden, in 2025, and a United States Smash was launched the same year. The US event is the hardest test of the model. In June 2026, as it began again, the South China Morning Post reported that many opening-day tickets were unsold and that seats were empty even for the singles finals. Tickets started at US$40.50 and the tournament carried a prize fund of US$1.55m. The contrast with China, where events sell out quickly, is the reason the expansion is expensive.

The expansion is meant to create revenue that does not depend on China. The ITTF's own statement presents WTT as a way to capture the sport's value and reinvest it. Steve Dainton has said that newer markets typically need a two to three year runway to mature commercially, while Chinese events can achieve success almost at once, as China Daily reported. That view is consistent with the US figures, and it is also a reason to ask how long the expansion can be funded.
## The question that is still open

China is the market that makes WTT's product look credible. It supplies the crowds, the sponsors, the television figures and the best players. The published accounts show that WTT's revenue has grown fast, from US$16m in 2019 to more than US$52m in 2024. They do not show where that revenue was earned, and they cannot show how much of it would survive without China's tournaments.

A breakdown of WTT's revenue by market would answer that question. Until one is published, the case that expansion is creating new commercial value, rather than being funded by China, will have to rest on trust. Part two looks at the accounts themselves, the money that comes in, and the questions the ITTF has yet to answer.
